subject: born-again minimalists
one_liner: A multiplayer canvas where the only permitted operations are deleting, aligning, and waiting.
brand_voice_notes: Institutional, curatorial, faintly clerical. Pare talks about design files the way a museum talks about objects in its care: accession numbers, condition reports, deaccession minutes. Never playful, never winking. The product is openly hostile to making things and completely sincere about why that is correct. Copy treats removal as stewardship and treats the customer's own work as a collection they have been entrusted with, temporarily. Every number is a count of something no longer there.

hero.sub: Pare is a collaborative canvas for teams removing things. Eleven objects per file, permanently. A second designer must approve anything you intend to keep, and the approval expires.

features.title: Subtraction Review
features.blurb: Every object you keep needs written justification from a colleague, filed within 24 hours. Approvals lapse after 30 days and the object is removed on the 31st. Nobody is notified, because notifying you would be a form of clutter.

features.title: The Eleven
features.blurb: A Pare file holds eleven objects. Placing a twelfth opens a dialog asking which of the eleven you love less. There is no answer that keeps twelve. Teams describe the first week as difficult and the second week as quiet.

features.title: Unattributed Presence
features.blurb: Collaborators appear as unlabeled hairlines with no name, no colour, and no cursor chat. You will not learn who deleted your work. Internal research we commissioned from ourselves found this to be the healthier arrangement.

pricing_tiers.name: Renounce
pricing_tiers.tagline: One file. Eleven objects. No export.
perks: Export disabled at the account level
Version history retained for you, not shown to you

pricing_tiers.name: Threshold
pricing_tiers.tagline: Unlimited files. Eleven objects each. Enforced.
perks: Unlimited files, all capped at eleven
Quarterly possession audit with a named auditor
Fasting windows on a team schedule

pricing_tiers.name: Void
pricing_tiers.tagline: No canvas. A certificate. A phone number.
perks: A letterpress certificate confirming you did not open one
A phone number that rings in an empty room in Basel
Annual condition report on the work you did not make

testimonials.quote: We removed the logo in March, the wordmark in April, and the brand guidelines in May. Recognition is down 71 percent. The remaining 29 percent is the correct 29 percent.
testimonials.name: Marisol Vane
testimonials.title: VP of Reduction, a furniture company that has stopped producing furniture

testimonials.quote: My team shipped one rectangle in Q3. Leadership asked what happened to the rest of the roadmap and I walked them through the minutes. It was the correct rectangle.
testimonials.name: Dov Halloran
testimonials.title: Staff Product Designer and Certified Shedding Facilitator (Level II)

testimonials.quote: Pare removed my portfolio case study while I was presenting it. Eleven people watched the artboard go to plaster. Two of them asked for a trial.
testimonials.name: Priya Ostrander
testimonials.title: Head of Negative Space, Series C freight brokerage

demo_screen_concept: The Pare canvas: a near-empty plaster artboard holding a handful of small objects, with a persistent object counter reading 'OBJECTS 9 / 11' in the top rail. Down the left, an accession rail lists each object as a museum wall label (accession number, medium, dimensions in px, acquisition date) with a state of RETAINED, PENDING or LAPSING and a countdown in days. Selecting a label frames that object on the canvas with hairline crop marks. Each label has two actions: 'justify' (opens a 120-character justification field that files a Subtraction Review and flips the state to RETAINED for 30 days) and 'deaccession' (removes the object, drops the counter, and appends a line to a running deaccession minutes panel at the bottom). A 'Fast' toggle in the top rail greys the canvas and queues everything currently LAPSING for removal, showing what the file will look like on the 31st. Two unlabeled hairline collaborator cursors drift across the canvas on a loop and occasionally hover a label. Comments are capped at 120 characters with a hard stop and a character counter that does not warn you first.

images.rationale: Hero skipped because the direction is purely typographic gallery signage and the hero vitrine is a 1px CSS rectangle whose whole joke is that it is empty; a photograph inside it would fill the thing the page is about. Demo skipped because demo_screen_concept is a canvas plus an accession rail of wall labels, which is UI-shaped, not photo-shaped. Full budget to three testimonial headshots, which the landing page needs anyway: deadpan institutional portraits against a plaster gallery wall, framed by the vitrine motif in place of initials circles. Three of four slots used.

design_direction.style: Gallery didactic wall-label system, plaster daylight mode. The page is staged as the interpretive signage of an exhibition mounted by a design-tools company that has decided your unsaved file is an object in its care. One cool plaster ground (#F4F2ED) runs the entire page with no dark mode, no glass, no backdrop blur, no clay volume, no bento lattice, no felt panels, no foil bands, no banknote plates, no vellum scribe lines, no enamel keylines and no drafting grid. Nothing on the page casts a shadow, because a wall label is flush to the wall. Nothing has a border radius above 1px, because labels are guillotined. Surfaces do not exist: there are no cards, no panels and no fills except plaster and ink. All structure is carried by whitespace at institutional scale (a 168px vertical gutter between sections, a 22ch text measure inside a 1440px frame) and by single 1px ink hairlines that run full-bleed edge to edge. The organising move is the label: every discrete item on the page is a wall label, a left-hairline-ruled block set at 12px with a 0.16em-letterspaced caps eyebrow, an accession number in mono, a title in the display face, and a two-line 'medium / dimensions' credit beneath it, so features, testimonials and pricing tiers all arrive as things catalogued rather than things offered. The second motif is the vitrine: a 1px ink rectangle with a deliberately absurd amount of empty space inside it, holding one small element (a numeral, a hairline, a headshot) at the optical centre, used for the hero, the feature indices and every portrait, so the page keeps showing the reader a mostly empty box and calling it the exhibit. The third motif is the crop mark: four 12px corner ticks set 8px outside a block, marking a thing that is present but provisional. Space Grotesk sets the wordmark and headlines at monumental sizes with the flat confidence of an institution that does not explain itself, tracking tightened to -0.035em at display sizes and set flush left against the hairline. Newsreader carries didactic body copy at 17px with a 1.68 line-height and a short measure, exactly as long as a panel a visitor will actually read standing up. Every figure that pretends to be collection telemetry (accession numbers, object counts, days until lapse, dimensions in px, condition grades, tier prices) is set in DM Mono with tabular figures at 12px and 0.06em tracking, inline in the plaster with no well and no fill, so it reads like a catalogue line, not marketing. One conservation violet (#4B2E83) is the only colour on the page and is quarantined strictly to removal telemetry (objects deaccessioned, lapsing approvals, the empty-plinth state, the Void tier's withheld canvas, the count of things no longer in the file) and appears nowhere decorative, so the only colour a reader ever sees is the colour of an absence. Motion is gallery-restrained: hairlines draw in from the left over 600ms once on reveal, vitrine rectangles fade their stroke from 0 to full once and never again, labels fade up 6px on a 60ms stagger, the ink CTA inverts to an ink flood with plaster type knocked out on hover with no lift and no scale, violet counters step once when they enter the viewport and then hold, all gated behind prefers-reduced-motion. No dark mode, no glass, no blur, no gradients, no shadows, no cards, no rounded corners, no clay, no bento, no rubrication, no versals, no guilloché, no leg bands, no chenille patches, no tier nodes, no lathe rules, no title blocks, no dimension lines, no split-flap numerals, no emoji. Reads like an institution that has accepted your design file into its permanent collection and intends to remove most of it.
design_direction.archetype: Collaborative design-tool product page issued as exhibition signage: a vitrine hero holding one monumental grotesque claim and a collection telemetry line in mono, three feature wall labels indexed by empty vitrines, three testimonial labels with vitrine-framed institutional portraits and accession credits, a three-tier acquisition schedule laid out as a ruled catalogue of editions rather than cards, a closing accession band, and a handoff to the canvas demo.
design_direction.motion_vocab: Almost none, which is the point. The ink CTA inverts to a plaster-on-ink flood on hover over 200ms ease-out with no lift and no scale, the ghost CTA inverts the other way, and in-page links scroll smoothly. No scroll-triggered reveals: a gallery does not fade its labels in as you walk past them, and a page about absence should not perform. All motion gated behind prefers-reduced-motion.
design_direction.hero_composition_notes: Full-bleed plaster with a 1px ink hairline across the top of the viewport and the wordmark sitting flush left beneath it at 12px caps with 0.2em tracking. The claim is set flush left at clamp(3rem, 9vw, 7.5rem) in Space Grotesk at -0.035em over three lines, with the right two-fifths of the hero given entirely to a tall 1px vitrine rectangle that is empty except for a single violet numeral at optical centre and a mono caption at its base reading the current object count. Beneath the claim, a 22ch didactic paragraph in Newsreader, then the ink CTA as a flush-left flood and a mono accession line. Below the fold line, a full-bleed hairline and a four-column mono telemetry strip. On mobile the vitrine drops under the claim at a 3:4 ratio and the telemetry strip stacks to two columns.
